questions.topic: Government as an Institution of the State
questions.stem: Which of the following is the machinery through which the will of the state is formulated, expressed and carried out?
questions.explanation: Government is the agency of the state that makes, executes and interprets its will; society and nation are wider groupings without that machinery.

questions.topic: Government as an Institution of the State
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an essential feature of a state?
questions.explanation: A state needs population, territory, government and sovereignty; an official religion is not required (Nigeria itself forbids a state religion).

questions.topic: Government as an Institution of the State
questions.stem: The main difference between the state and the government is that the state is
options: made up only of elected officials
permanent while governments change from time to time
questions.explanation: Governments come and go through elections or other means, but the state continues as a permanent political entity.

questions.topic: Government as a Process or Art of Governing
questions.stem: Government as a process refers to
options: the buildings where public servants work
the activities by which policies are made and carried out
the total population of a country
questions.explanation: As a process, government means the art or activity of governing: making, implementing and enforcing decisions.

questions.topic: Government as a Process or Art of Governing
questions.stem: When a state governor signs a bill into law and directs ministries to implement it, government is being viewed as
options: a process or art of governing
questions.explanation: The act of making and carrying out decisions illustrates government as a process.

questions.topic: Government as an Academic Field of Study
questions.stem: Government as an academic field of study is mainly concerned with
options: the study of the state, its institutions and political behaviour
the training of soldiers for war
the study of plants and animals
questions.explanation: As a discipline, government studies political institutions, processes, ideas and behaviour.

questions.topic: Government as an Academic Field of Study
questions.stem: A student who compares how the legislatures of Ghana and Nigeria check the executive is engaging mainly in
questions.explanation: Comparing political institutions across countries is the branch called comparative politics.

questions.stem: The ability to compel obedience, if necessary by the use of force, is known as
questions.explanation: Power is the capacity to make others act as one wishes, even by force; authority is power that is recognised as rightful.

questions.stem: Power that is accepted as rightful by those over whom it is exercised is called
questions.explanation: Authority is legitimate power: the right to command, which the governed accept.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains legitimacy?
options: The supreme power of the state over its territory
The acceptance by the people of the right of a government to rule
The power of the courts to declare laws void
The use of force to maintain law and order
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is the popular acceptance of a government's right to exercise power; sovereignty is supreme power.

questions.stem: Sovereignty means the
options: right of citizens to vote at elections
supreme power of the state to make and enforce laws without external control
power of the judiciary to interpret the constitution
freedom of the press from censorship
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the supreme, final legal authority of the state within its territory and independence from outside control.

questions.stem: Which of the following limits the sovereignty of Nigeria in practice?
options: The existence of a written constitution
Its obligations under treaties of international organisations it has joined
The use of English as official language
questions.explanation: Membership of bodies such as the UN and ECOWAS imposes obligations that restrict a state's freedom of action, an external limitation on sovereignty.

questions.stem: A group of people bound together by common descent, language, culture and history is called a
questions.explanation: A nation is a cultural community; a state is a political-legal entity with territory and sovereignty.

questions.stem: The process by which people acquire political values, attitudes and beliefs is called
questions.explanation: Political socialization is the learning process (through family, school, peers, media and others) that forms political attitudes.

questions.stem: The sum of the attitudes, beliefs and values that people hold about their political system is known as
questions.explanation: Political culture is the shared pattern of political orientations in a society; socialization is how it is passed on.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an agent of political socialization?
questions.explanation: Family, school, peer groups, religious bodies, the media and political parties transmit political values.

questions.stem: Government by a small group of people who rule mainly in their own interest is called
questions.explanation: Oligarchy is rule by a few, usually the wealthy or powerful, for their own benefit.

questions.stem: Government by a privileged few believed to be the best qualified, often by birth, is known as
questions.explanation: Aristocracy literally means rule by the best, traditionally a hereditary noble class; plutocracy is rule by the rich.

questions.stem: A system in which land was held by lords who granted it to vassals in return for service and loyalty was
questions.explanation: Feudalism was based on land tenure in exchange for military service and loyalty, with serfs working the land.

questions.stem: Communalism as a system is characterised by
options: private ownership of factories by individuals
collective ownership of the means of production and sharing of produce
the existence of a strong middle class
questions.explanation: In communalism, land and resources belong to the community and members share the proceeds, as in many traditional African societies.

questions.stem: According to Karl Marx, the final stage of social development in which the state withers away is
questions.explanation: Marx saw socialism as a transitional stage leading to a classless, stateless communist society.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of socialism but NOT of capitalism?
options: State ownership and control of the major means of production
questions.explanation: Socialism places the commanding heights of the economy under public ownership; capitalism relies on private ownership.

questions.stem: A system in which the government controls every aspect of the life of the citizens is described as
questions.explanation: Totalitarianism seeks total control of political, economic, social and even private life.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a core belief of liberalism?
questions.explanation: Liberalism stresses individual rights, freedom of choice, rule of law and a government whose powers are limited.

questions.stem: The principle that no one is above the law is known as
questions.explanation: Rule of law means the supremacy of law and equality of all before it.

questions.stem: The rule of law was popularised by the British jurist
questions.explanation: A. V. Dicey expounded the rule of law in his 1885 work on the law of the constitution.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation on the rule of law in Nigeria?
options: Fair hearing in the law courts
The immunity from civil and criminal proceedings granted to the President and Governors while in office
questions.explanation: Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution shields certain office holders from prosecution while in office, which departs from equality before the law.

questions.stem: The theory of separation of powers is associated with
questions.explanation: Montesquieu set out the doctrine in The Spirit of the Laws (1748).

questions.stem: The power of the Nigerian President to veto a bill passed by the National Assembly is an example of
questions.explanation: The veto lets the executive check the legislature; the National Assembly can in turn override it by a two-thirds majority.

questions.stem: The power of the courts to declare an act of the legislature or executive unconstitutional is called
questions.explanation: Judicial review allows the courts to strike down laws and actions that conflict with the constitution.

questions.stem: In which of the following systems is the fusion rather than separation of powers most evident?
questions.explanation: In the parliamentary system ministers are members of the legislature, so executive and legislative powers are fused.

questions.stem: Laws made by bodies other than the legislature under powers granted by the legislature are called
questions.explanation: Delegated legislation includes bye-laws, orders, rules and regulations made under authority given by an enabling act.

questions.stem: A major reason for delegated legislation is that
options: it removes the need for a constitution
it allows courts to make laws
the legislature lacks time and technical knowledge to make every detailed rule
questions.explanation: Legislatures pass broad laws and allow ministers, councils and agencies with expertise to fill in technical details.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a control over delegated legislation?
options: The power of the courts to declare it ultra vires
The power of the President to dissolve the courts
The use of referendum for every bye-law
questions.explanation: Courts can void delegated legislation that goes beyond the powers granted (ultra vires); the legislature can also amend or revoke it.

questions.stem: Fundamental human rights are
options: privileges granted only to party members
duties owed by citizens to the state
basic rights to which every person is entitled by virtue of being human
rights enjoyed only by public servants
questions.explanation: Fundamental human rights belong to all people because they are human; Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution protects them.

questions.stem: Fundamental human rights in the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria are contained in
questions.explanation: Chapter IV (sections 33 to 46) guarantees fundamental rights; Chapter II contains the fundamental objectives and directive principles.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, an individual whose fundamental right has been infringed may apply for redress to
options: a High Court in the state where the infringement occurred
questions.explanation: Section 46 gives any person who alleges a breach of a fundamental right the right to apply to a High Court in that state for redress.

questions.stem: Constitutionalism means
options: the act of writing a constitution
the abolition of the constitution by the military
government according to the provisions of the constitution, with limits on power
the power of the President to make any law
questions.explanation: Constitutionalism is the idea that government power is limited by, and exercised according to, the constitution.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a form of political participation?
questions.explanation: Political participation includes voting, contesting, campaigning, joining parties and petitioning government.

questions.stem: When a federal ministry posts its own officers to state capitals to carry out federal functions without transferring decision-making authority, this is
questions.explanation: Deconcentration is administrative decentralization: central officials operate in the field, but authority stays at the centre.

questions.stem: A constitution may be defined as
options: a list of the members of the cabinet
the body of fundamental rules and principles according to which a state is governed
the manifesto of the ruling party
the annual budget of the government
questions.explanation: A constitution sets out how a state is organised, how power is distributed and the rights of citizens.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a source of a constitution?
questions.explanation: Sources include statutes, judicial precedents, conventions, customs, historical documents and the works of learned writers.

questions.stem: Rules of political behaviour which are not written in law but are observed because they have been accepted over time are called
questions.explanation: Constitutional conventions, important in Britain, are customary practices that are binding in practice though not legally enforceable.

questions.stem: Which of the following bodies produced the draft of the 1979 Constitution of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: A Constitution Drafting Committee (1975-1976) produced the draft, which a Constituent Assembly then debated.

questions.stem: A main function of a constitution is to
options: fix the prices of goods in the market
define the powers of the organs of government and their relationships
questions.explanation: A constitution establishes the organs of government, allocates their powers and regulates their relationships.

questions.stem: A constitution limits arbitrary rule chiefly by
options: allowing the executive to suspend the courts
making the head of state a monarch
specifying the powers and limits of public office holders
questions.explanation: By stating what each organ may and may not do, a constitution restrains abuse of power.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the constitution of a federal state?
options: Creating a single centre of power
Dividing powers between the central and the regional governments
Making the President the sole law-maker
questions.explanation: A federal constitution divides legislative powers between levels, as Nigeria does through the exclusive and concurrent lists.

questions.stem: A constitution whose provisions are contained in a single document is called
questions.explanation: A written constitution is codified in one or a few documents, like Nigeria's.

questions.stem: Which of the following countries is a classic example of a country with an unwritten constitution?
questions.explanation: Britain's constitution is not codified in one document; it rests on statutes, conventions, judicial decisions and historical documents.

questions.stem: A constitution that requires a special and difficult procedure for its amendment is said to be
questions.explanation: A rigid constitution cannot be amended in the same way as ordinary law, as with Nigeria's section 9 procedure.

questions.stem: A flexible constitution is one that
options: must be amended by a referendum
can be amended in the same way as ordinary laws
can be amended only by the courts
questions.explanation: Flexible constitutions, such as Britain's, are amended by ordinary legislative procedure.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, an ordinary amendment requires the support of two-thirds of the members of each House of the National Assembly and approval by resolution of the Houses of Assembly of
options: a simple majority of the states
not less than two-thirds of all the states
questions.explanation: Section 9(2) requires two-thirds in each House of the National Assembly and approval by the Houses of Assembly of at least two-thirds of the states (24 of 36).

questions.stem: To alter Chapter IV (fundamental rights) of the 1999 Constitution, each House of the National Assembly must support the bill by not less than
options: a simple majority of members present
questions.explanation: Section 9(3) sets a stricter four-fifths requirement for changing section 8, section 9 itself or Chapter IV, plus approval by two-thirds of the state Houses of Assembly.

questions.stem: The organ of government responsible for making laws is the
questions.explanation: The legislature makes laws; the executive implements them and the judiciary interprets them.

questions.stem: The organ of government that interprets laws and settles disputes is the
questions.explanation: The judiciary interprets laws and adjudicates disputes between persons and between persons and the state.

questions.stem: The Nigerian National Assembly consists of the
options: Senate and the House of Representatives
Senate and the Federal Executive Council
House of Representatives and the Council of State
House of Chiefs and the Senate
questions.explanation: Nigeria has a bicameral federal legislature: the Senate and the House of Representatives.

questions.stem: How many members make up the Senate of Nigeria under the 1999 Constitution?
questions.explanation: Each of the 36 states has three senators and the FCT has one: 36 x 3 + 1 = 109.

questions.stem: The House of Representatives of Nigeria is made up of
questions.explanation: The constitution fixes the House at 360 members elected from federal constituencies; together with 109 senators the National Assembly has 469 members.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the legislature?
questions.explanation: The legislature appropriates public funds by passing the appropriation (budget) bill.

questions.stem: The process of removing the President of Nigeria from office by the National Assembly for gross misconduct is called
questions.explanation: Impeachment under section 143 requires a two-thirds majority of each House after an investigating panel finds the allegation proved.

questions.stem: In Nigeria, a bill vetoed by the President becomes law if it is passed again by each House of the National Assembly by
questions.explanation: Section 58(5) allows the National Assembly to override a presidential veto by a two-thirds majority in each House.

questions.stem: The highest court in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court is the final court of appeal in Nigeria.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, the Chief Justice of Nigeria is appointed by the President on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council, subject to confirmation by the
questions.explanation: Section 231 requires Senate confirmation of the CJN's appointment.

questions.stem: Which of the following promotes the independence of the judiciary?
options: Appointment of judges by party leaders
Payment of judges' salaries at the President's discretion
Removal of judges by the Governor at will
questions.explanation: Security of tenure, salaries charged on the Consolidated Revenue Fund and appointment through the judicial council insulate judges from pressure.

questions.stem: The salaries of Nigerian judges are charged on the Consolidated Revenue Fund in order to
options: allow judges to fix their own salaries
make judges members of the civil service
allow states to pay federal judges
protect judges from financial pressure by the executive or legislature
questions.explanation: Charging salaries on the Consolidated Revenue Fund means they are not voted annually, so they cannot be used to punish judges.

questions.stem: A legislature with only one chamber is described as
questions.explanation: Unicameral legislatures have one chamber; Nigeria's state Houses of Assembly are unicameral.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A system of government in which powers are constitutionally shared between a central government and component units is
questions.explanation: Federalism divides power between central and regional governments, each supreme in its own sphere.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: In a unitary system of government,
options: there must be two legislative chambers
all powers are concentrated in the central government
the head of state must be a monarch
questions.explanation: Under a unitary system, local units exercise only powers delegated by the central government.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: In a confederation,
options: there is only one level of government
the component units are stronger than the central authority
questions.explanation: Confederal units retain their sovereignty and can usually withdraw; the centre is weak.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: Which of the following is a merit of the unitary system?
options: It protects the interests of minority groups
It is suitable for large and diverse countries
It ensures quick decision-making and a strong government
questions.explanation: A single centre of authority allows speedy, uniform decisions; it suits small, homogeneous countries.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A feature of the presidential system of government is that
options: the cabinet is collectively responsible to parliament
the head of government is a member of the legislature
the legislature can be dissolved by the President at will
the President is both head of state and head of government
questions.explanation: In a presidential system one person combines both headships, as in Nigeria and the USA.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: In the parliamentary system, the government of the day can be removed by
options: a decision of the Supreme Court
a vote of no confidence in the legislature
a declaration by the head of state alone
the expiry of the Prime Minister's fixed term only
questions.explanation: The cabinet depends on the confidence of the legislature; losing a vote of no confidence forces resignation or dissolution.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: Collective responsibility is a feature of the
questions.explanation: Cabinet members in a parliamentary system publicly support cabinet decisions and fall together if defeated.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: A system in which the head of state inherits the office is known as
questions.explanation: In a monarchy the head of state (king or queen) succeeds by inheritance.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem: Which of the following countries operates a constitutional monarchy?
questions.explanation: Britain's monarch reigns but does not rule; power is exercised by ministers responsible to Parliament.

questions.stem: A citizen is
options: a full member of a state entitled to its rights and bound by its obligations
a person who holds a public office
an alien resident in a country
questions.explanation: Citizenship is legal membership of a state, carrying full rights and duties.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, Nigerian citizenship can be acquired by birth, by registration and by
options: residence in Nigeria for one year
questions.explanation: Sections 25 to 27 provide for citizenship by birth, registration and naturalisation.

questions.stem: A foreign woman who is or has been married to a citizen of Nigeria may become a Nigerian citizen by
questions.explanation: Section 26 allows registration for a woman who is or has been married to a Nigerian citizen, among others.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a civic obligation of a Nigerian citizen?
questions.explanation: Obligations include obeying laws, paying taxes, defending the country and respecting others' rights; joining a party is a right, not a duty.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a political right of a citizen?
options: The right to vote and be voted for
The right to free medical care abroad
The right to own a car
The right to a free university degree
questions.explanation: Political rights include voting, contesting elections and holding public office.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, a person who acquired Nigerian citizenship by registration or naturalisation may be
options: deprived of it only by a local government council
deprived of it by the President in circumstances such as disloyalty or a prison sentence within a set period
never deprived of it under any circumstances
deprived of it automatically on travelling abroad
questions.explanation: Section 30 permits deprivation, but only for citizens by registration or naturalisation, not for citizens by birth.

questions.stem: A political party is an organised group of people whose main aim is to
options: win elections and control the government
questions.explanation: Unlike pressure groups, political parties seek to capture and exercise governmental power through elections.

questions.stem: The document in which a political party sets out what it intends to do if elected is its
questions.explanation: A manifesto states the party's programmes and promises to the electorate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of political parties?
options: Aggregating interests and presenting candidates for elections
Interpreting the laws of the land
questions.explanation: Parties recruit and present candidates, aggregate interests and educate voters; voter registration is the electoral body's job.

questions.stem: The organ of a party that runs its day-to-day affairs is usually the
questions.explanation: The secretariat handles routine administration; the national convention is the supreme organ that meets periodically.

questions.stem: A cadre party differs from a mass party in that a cadre party
options: has membership open to all adults
relies on a small group of influential notables rather than a large membership
depends mainly on membership dues from the masses
questions.explanation: Cadre (elite) parties are built around prominent individuals; mass parties seek large paying memberships.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, a political association in Nigeria shall not function as a party unless, among other conditions,
options: its name, symbol or logo does not have any ethnic or religious connotation
it is founded by a serving military officer
its membership is limited to one state
its headquarters is located outside Abuja
questions.explanation: Section 222 requires an open membership, a constitution registered with INEC, headquarters in the FCT and a name and symbol without ethnic or religious meaning.

questions.stem: A party system in which only two major parties compete for power is called
questions.explanation: Two dominant parties alternate in power, as in the United States.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of the multi-party system?
options: It always produces a stable majority government
It gives voters a wide choice of programmes and candidates
It is the cheapest system to operate
questions.explanation: Many parties offer varied alternatives, though they may produce unstable coalitions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely in a multi-party parliamentary system where no party wins an outright majority?
questions.explanation: When no party has a majority, parties combine to form a coalition government.

questions.stem: A pressure group is an organised group that seeks to
options: influence government policy without seeking to control government
questions.explanation: Pressure groups influence policy in favour of their members' interests but do not field candidates for power.

questions.stem: The method by which pressure groups try to persuade legislators to support their interests is known as
questions.explanation: Lobbying is direct contact with law-makers and officials to influence decisions.

questions.stem: A pressure group formed to protect the economic interests of its members, such as a trade union, is called
questions.explanation: Interest or protective groups defend the material interests of members; promotional groups champion causes.

questions.stem: A sudden, spontaneous protest by aggrieved people with no formal organisation is an example of
questions.explanation: Anomic groups emerge spontaneously, often as riots or demonstrations, without formal structure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a difference between a pressure group and a political party?
options: A pressure group does not contest elections to form a government
A pressure group has no members
A political party never influences policy
A political party is always illegal
questions.explanation: Parties seek to control government; pressure groups only influence it.

questions.stem: A major function of pressure groups in a democracy is to
options: articulate the interests of their members to government
questions.explanation: Pressure groups bring the views and demands of sections of society to the attention of policy-makers.

questions.stem: Public opinion refers to
options: the opinion of the President alone
the views held by a significant section of the people on public issues
the judgement of the Supreme Court
a law passed by the legislature
questions.explanation: Public opinion is the aggregate of views held by members of the public on issues of general concern.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a method of measuring public opinion?
questions.explanation: Opinion polls, elections, referendums, letters and protests reveal public opinion.

questions.stem: Public opinion is important in a democracy mainly because it
options: guides government on the wishes of the people and keeps it accountable
questions.explanation: Governments that ignore public opinion risk losing legitimacy and elections.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of electronic mass media?
questions.explanation: Radio, television and internet platforms are electronic media; newspapers and magazines are print media.

questions.stem: The press is often described as the fourth estate of the realm because it
options: acts as a watchdog over the other arms of government
questions.explanation: As the fourth estate the press informs the public and checks the executive, legislature and judiciary.

questions.stem: A negative effect of the mass media on politics is that it may
options: spread false information and inflame tensions
questions.explanation: Irresponsible reporting and fake news can mislead voters and heighten conflict.

questions.stem: The right to vote is known as
questions.explanation: Franchise or suffrage is the right to vote in elections.

questions.stem: The minimum voting age in Nigeria is
questions.explanation: Nigerian citizens aged 18 and above may register and vote.

questions.stem: Universal adult suffrage means that
options: all qualified adult citizens may vote irrespective of sex, wealth or education
questions.explanation: Universal adult suffrage extends the vote to all adult citizens subject only to minimal conditions like age and sanity.

questions.stem: The electoral system in which the candidate with the highest number of votes wins, even without an absolute majority, is
questions.explanation: First-past-the-post awards the seat to whoever has the most votes, not necessarily over 50 per cent.

questions.stem: A major advantage of proportional representation is that it
options: gives small parties seats in proportion to their votes
is the simplest system to understand
creates strong links between a member and a single constituency
questions.explanation: Proportional representation reflects the distribution of votes, so minority parties win representation.

questions.stem: Under the 1999 Constitution, to be declared President at the first ballot a candidate must have the highest number of votes and at least one-quarter of the votes cast in
options: all the states and the Federal Capital Territory
a simple majority of the states
at least two-thirds of all the states and the Federal Capital Territory
questions.explanation: Section 134(2) sets a spread requirement of 25 per cent of votes in at least two-thirds of the states and the FCT.

questions.stem: The deliberate drawing of constituency boundaries to favour a particular party is called
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering manipulates boundaries to give one party an advantage.

questions.stem: A vote taken by the electorate to decide directly on a specific issue is a
questions.explanation: A referendum lets the electorate accept or reject a proposal directly.

questions.stem: An election held to fill a vacancy that occurs between two general elections is a
questions.explanation: A by-election fills a seat left vacant through death, resignation or removal.

questions.stem: The body responsible for conducting federal elections in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: INEC organises, undertakes and supervises federal and state elections.

questions.stem: State Independent Electoral Commissions in Nigeria are responsible for conducting
questions.explanation: Under the 1999 Constitution, each state's SIEC conducts local government elections.

questions.stem: Which of the following bodies conducted elections in Nigeria's Second Republic?
questions.explanation: FEDECO, created in 1978, conducted the 1979 and 1983 elections; INEC was established in 1998.

questions.stem: The independence of INEC is promoted by the fact that its Chairman and members
options: are appointed by the political parties
can be removed only on an address supported by two-thirds of the Senate
are elected by the voters every two years
may be removed by the President at will
questions.explanation: Section 157 requires a Senate address supported by two-thirds of members before the President can remove an INEC member, which protects tenure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of the civil service?
questions.explanation: Civil servants are expected to be neutral, anonymous, permanent and impartial.

questions.stem: The administrative head of a federal ministry in Nigeria is the
options: Head of the Civil Service of the Federation
questions.explanation: The Minister is the political head; the Permanent Secretary is the administrative head and accounting officer.

questions.stem: The principle of anonymity in the civil service means that
options: civil servants are not publicly blamed or praised for the policies they help to make
civil servants do not have names in official records
civil servants are not paid salaries
questions.explanation: Ministers take public responsibility for policy, so civil servants remain anonymous.

questions.stem: The Federal Civil Service Commission in Nigeria is responsible for
options: appointment, promotion and discipline of federal civil servants
questions.explanation: The Commission handles appointment, promotion and discipline in the federal civil service.

questions.stem: The main reason for creating a civil service commission is to
options: give ministers power to hire their supporters
insulate appointments and discipline in the service from political interference
questions.explanation: An independent commission promotes merit and protects civil servants from political pressure.

questions.stem: Public corporations are established mainly to
options: provide essential services that private firms may not adequately provide
make maximum profit for private owners
questions.explanation: They provide utilities and strategic services, often at affordable prices, in the public interest.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a means of controlling public corporations?
options: Ministerial control through the supervising ministry
questions.explanation: Corporations are controlled through ministers, the legislature, the courts, audits and public opinion.

questions.stem: The sale of government shares in a public enterprise to private investors is known as
questions.explanation: Privatization transfers ownership; commercialization keeps ownership but runs the enterprise for profit.

questions.stem: Commercialization of a public enterprise means that the enterprise
options: remains government-owned but is run on a profit-making basis
is sold completely to private owners
is handed over to a foreign country
questions.explanation: Commercialization makes a state enterprise operate like a business without changing its ownership.

questions.stem: Local government is the
options: third tier of government closest to the people
same thing as the civil service
questions.explanation: In Nigeria, local government is the third tier after the federal and state governments.

questions.stem: How many local government areas are listed in the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: The First Schedule lists 774 local government areas.

questions.stem: The 1976 local government reform in Nigeria introduced
options: a uniform, single-tier, multi-purpose local government system
two-tier local governments in each state
questions.explanation: The 1976 reform made local government a uniform, single-tier third level of government nationwide.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a major problem of local governments in Nigeria?
options: Absence of elections in the constitution
questions.explanation: Undue state interference, inadequate funds and corruption weaken local governments.

questions.stem: In the pre-colonial Hausa/Fulani political system, the head of the emirate was the
questions.explanation: Each emirate was headed by an Emir who owed allegiance to the Sultan of Sokoto or the Emir of Gwandu.

questions.stem: In the pre-colonial Hausa/Fulani system, the official who acted as the Emir's chief adviser, similar to a prime minister, was the
questions.explanation: The Waziri was chief adviser; the Madawaki commanded the army; the Alkali was a judge.

questions.stem: The Alkali in the Hausa/Fulani emirate system was in charge of
options: the administration of justice according to Islamic law
questions.explanation: Alkalis presided over Sharia courts.

questions.stem: In the old Oyo Empire, the Alaafin's powers were checked mainly by the
questions.explanation: The Oyomesi, a council of seven kingmakers led by the Bashorun, could ask an Alaafin to commit suicide if he lost their confidence.

questions.stem: The head of the Oyomesi in the old Oyo Empire was the
questions.explanation: The Bashorun led the Oyomesi and was the most powerful chief after the Alaafin.

questions.stem: Which body in the old Oyo political system served as a check on the Oyomesi?
questions.explanation: The Ogboni, an earth cult, mediated between the Alaafin and the Oyomesi and checked the latter.

questions.stem: Which of the following institutions in traditional Igbo society performed functions such as clearing paths and enforcing community decisions?
questions.explanation: Age grades carried out public works, policing and defence in Igbo communities.

questions.stem: A major difference between the pre-colonial Hausa/Fulani and Igbo political systems was that
options: the Hausa/Fulani system was centralized while the Igbo system was largely decentralized
the Igbo system was based on Islamic law
questions.explanation: The emirates had a centralized hierarchy; Igbo communities governed themselves through dispersed institutions.

questions.stem: The system by which the British ruled through traditional rulers and institutions was called
questions.explanation: Indirect rule used existing chiefs and institutions under British supervision.

questions.stem: Indirect rule in Nigeria is most closely associated with
questions.explanation: Lugard applied indirect rule in Northern Nigeria and later throughout the country.

questions.stem: A major reason for the adoption of indirect rule in Northern Nigeria was
options: the shortage of British personnel and funds
the large number of missionaries in the North
questions.explanation: Few officials, limited funds and the existence of a well-organised emirate system made indirect rule convenient.

questions.stem: Indirect rule was least successful in
questions.explanation: Most Igbo communities lacked centralized rulers, so the British created unpopular warrant chiefs.

questions.stem: The Aba Women's Riot of 1929 was a reaction mainly against
options: the rumoured extension of taxation to women and the conduct of warrant chiefs
the transfer of the capital to Abuja
questions.explanation: Women protested against rumoured taxation and abuses by warrant chiefs, exposing the failure of indirect rule in the East.

questions.stem: The French policy aimed at turning Africans into Frenchmen in culture and outlook was
questions.explanation: Assimilation sought to make colonial subjects French in language, culture and law.

questions.stem: The Loi Cadre of 1956 in French West Africa
options: created a single federation government with full independence
made Dakar part of mainland France
introduced universal suffrage and gave more powers to territorial assemblies
questions.explanation: The 1956 framework law extended the vote and strengthened territorial assemblies, which tended to break up the federation.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a feature of French colonial administration?
options: A highly centralized system in which chiefs were mere agents of the administration
Strong native authorities with independent treasuries
Rule through emirs who kept their sovereignty
questions.explanation: French chiefs were appointed officials subordinate to French administrators, unlike British native authorities.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a positive effect of colonial rule in Nigeria?
options: Exploitation of mineral resources for Britain
questions.explanation: Western education, modern transport and a unified administrative framework are commonly cited benefits.

questions.stem: A negative economic effect of colonial rule was that
options: colonies were made producers of raw materials for European industries
industries were spread evenly in all regions
questions.explanation: Colonial economies were geared to export primary products and import manufactured goods.

questions.stem: Nationalism in Nigeria refers to
options: the expansion of the Oyo Empire
the conflict between political parties after 1999
the struggle by Nigerians to end colonial rule and achieve self-government
questions.explanation: Nigerian nationalism was the movement against colonial domination for independence.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors encouraged nationalism in Nigeria?
options: The return of ex-servicemen after the Second World War
questions.explanation: Ex-servicemen, Western-educated elites, the press and Pan-African ideas all fed nationalism.

questions.stem: The West African Pilot, a newspaper that promoted nationalism, was founded in 1937 by
questions.explanation: Azikiwe's West African Pilot became a leading nationalist paper.

questions.stem: The motion for self-government in 1956 moved in the House of Representatives in 1953 was tabled by
questions.explanation: Enahoro's 1953 motion was opposed by northern members and led to the crisis that ended the Macpherson Constitution.

questions.stem: The organisation formed in 1934, which later became the first nationalist movement with a national outlook, was the
options: Lagos Youth Movement, later the Nigerian Youth Movement
questions.explanation: The Lagos Youth Movement (1934) became the Nigerian Youth Movement in 1936.

questions.stem: The constitution that introduced the elective principle in Nigeria was the
questions.explanation: The Clifford Constitution provided for elected members from Lagos and Calabar.

questions.stem: Under the Clifford Constitution, the elected members of the Legislative Council came from
questions.explanation: Three members were elected from Lagos and one from Calabar.

questions.stem: The Richards Constitution of 1946 is noted for
options: introducing regionalism with three regional houses
questions.explanation: The Richards Constitution created Northern, Western and Eastern regions with regional Houses of Assembly.

questions.stem: A major criticism of the Richards Constitution by nationalists was that
options: it was imposed without consulting Nigerians
it made Nigeria independent too early
questions.explanation: Nationalists objected to the lack of consultation and the limited role of elected Africans.

questions.stem: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 was the first to
options: establish the Supreme Court as final court
involve wide consultation with Nigerians before it was drafted
questions.explanation: Consultations from village level to the Ibadan General Conference of 1950 preceded it.

questions.stem: The Macpherson Constitution broke down largely because of
options: the outbreak of the civil war
the crisis over the 1953 self-government motion
questions.explanation: The disagreement over the self-government motion and the Kano riots exposed its weaknesses.

questions.stem: Nigeria became independent on
questions.explanation: Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 and a republic on 1 October 1963.

questions.stem: Under the 1960 Independence Constitution, Nigeria's final court of appeal was the
options: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London
questions.explanation: Appeals to the Privy Council ended with the Republican Constitution of 1963.

questions.stem: The 1963 Republican Constitution of Nigeria
options: replaced the British monarch with a Nigerian President as head of state
questions.explanation: The ceremonial President replaced the Queen; executive power remained with the Prime Minister.

questions.stem: The 1979 Constitution of Nigeria introduced
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution adopted an American-style executive presidency.

questions.stem: Nigeria's current constitution came into force on
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution came into force on 29 May 1999 with the start of the Fourth Republic.

questions.stem: A criticism of the 1999 Constitution is that it
options: has no provisions on fundamental rights
was prepared under military rule and claims to be made by 'the people'
questions.explanation: Critics note the contrast between its military origin and its preamble 'We the people'. It has been amended several times.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The Action Group was founded in 1951 under the leadership of
questions.explanation: The Action Group grew out of the Egbe Omo Oduduwa cultural association.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The Northern People's Congress (NPC) was led by
questions.explanation: The Sardauna of Sokoto, Ahmadu Bello, led the NPC.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The NCNC was formed in 1944 as the
options: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons
questions.explanation: It was so named because the British Cameroons was administered with Nigeria.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU) was led by
questions.explanation: NEPU, founded in 1950, was a radical northern party led by Mallam Aminu Kano.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: The United Middle Belt Congress (UMBC) drew most of its support from
options: minority groups in the Middle Belt of the Northern Region
questions.explanation: Led by Joseph Tarka, the UMBC championed Middle Belt minorities.

questions.topic: Development of Major Political Parties in Nigeria
questions.stem: A common weakness of the major parties of Nigeria's First Republic was that they
options: were largely based on regional and ethnic support
questions.explanation: Each major party dominated one region, which deepened ethnic politics.

questions.stem: The first military coup in Nigeria took place on
questions.explanation: The coup of 15 January 1966 ended the First Republic.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of military rule?
options: An active opposition party in parliament
questions.explanation: Military regimes suspend parts of the constitution and govern by decrees (federal) and edicts (state).

questions.stem: Unification Decree No. 34 of 1966
options: abolished the federal structure and introduced a unitary system
questions.explanation: Decree 34 under the Ironsi regime replaced federalism with a unitary system, increasing tension.

questions.stem: Nigeria's twelve-state structure was created in
questions.explanation: The twelve states were created in May 1967, shortly before the civil war.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a reason commonly given by military officers for intervening in Nigerian politics?
options: The demand of the United Nations
Corruption and political instability under civilian governments
The wish to establish a monarchy
questions.explanation: Coup plotters typically cited corruption, electoral malpractice and insecurity.

questions.stem: Under military rule in Nigeria, the highest law-making body was variously called the Supreme Military Council, the Armed Forces Ruling Council and the
questions.explanation: Each regime gave its supreme body a name; the last was the Provisional Ruling Council.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: Nigeria adopted the federal system mainly because of its
options: large size and ethnic and cultural diversity
questions.explanation: Federalism accommodates diversity while keeping the country together.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: The list containing matters on which only the National Assembly can legislate is the
questions.explanation: Matters such as defence, foreign affairs and currency are on the Exclusive List.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: Matters on which both the federal and state legislatures can make laws are contained in the
questions.explanation: The Concurrent List covers matters such as education and electricity; federal law prevails in a conflict.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: Which of the following is on the Exclusive Legislative List of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.explanation: Defence, currency, foreign affairs and citizenship are exclusively federal.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: Powers not listed in either the exclusive or the concurrent list, which belong to the states, are called
questions.explanation: Residual matters, such as chieftaincy, are for the states.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: The principle that the composition of government agencies should reflect the diversity of Nigeria is called
questions.explanation: Section 14(3) of the constitution requires government to reflect the federal character of Nigeria.

questions.topic: Federal System of Government in Nigeria
questions.stem: Nigeria currently has how many states?
questions.explanation: Nigeria has 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.

questions.stem: Foreign policy is
options: the policy on foreign workers only
the way a state raises taxes
the set of principles guiding a country's relations with other countries
questions.explanation: Foreign policy covers the goals and strategies a state pursues in dealing with other states.

questions.stem: Africa has been described as the centrepiece of Nigeria's foreign policy because Nigeria
options: gives priority to African unity, liberation and development
is the only African member of the UN
was the founder of the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: Since independence Nigeria has placed African interests at the centre of its external relations.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a principle of Nigeria's foreign policy?
options: Non-interference in the internal affairs of other states
Expansion of Nigeria's territory by force
questions.explanation: Nigeria's principles include non-alignment, non-interference, respect for sovereignty and peaceful settlement of disputes.

questions.stem: Nigeria broke diplomatic relations with France in 1961 in protest against
options: France's refusal to join the UN
French support for the civil war
French atomic tests in the Sahara
questions.explanation: The atomic tests in the Sahara led to the breaking of relations in January 1961.

questions.stem: The Technical Aid Corps scheme of Nigeria involves
options: training foreign soldiers in Nigeria only
sending Nigerian professionals to serve in other developing countries
exporting crude oil free of charge
questions.explanation: Under the scheme, set up in 1987, Nigerian volunteers serve in African, Caribbean and Pacific countries.

questions.stem: Nigeria's leading role in the ECOWAS Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) in the 1990s was mainly to
options: restore peace in Liberia and Sierra Leone
protect Nigerian oil in the Gulf of Guinea
questions.explanation: ECOMOG intervened in the civil wars of Liberia (from 1990) and Sierra Leone.

questions.stem: In 1979, Nigeria nationalised the assets of British Petroleum in Nigeria as a way of
options: punishing Britain for the civil war
pressing Britain over the independence of Zimbabwe (Rhodesia)
forcing Britain to leave the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: The nationalisation was meant to influence British policy on majority rule in Rhodesia.

questions.stem: The United Nations Organization came into existence in
questions.explanation: The UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.

questions.stem: The headquarters of the United Nations is in
questions.explanation: The UN headquarters is in New York; some agencies are in Geneva and elsewhere.

questions.stem: The organ of the UN primarily responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security is the
questions.explanation: The Security Council has primary responsibility for peace and security and can authorise enforcement action.

questions.stem: The permanent members of the UN Security Council are the USA, the UK, France, Russia and
questions.explanation: These five permanent members each hold a veto.

questions.stem: The judicial organ of the United Nations, the International Court of Justice, sits at
questions.explanation: The ICJ sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands.

questions.stem: The Organisation of African Unity was founded in 1963 in
questions.explanation: The OAU Charter was signed in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963.

questions.stem: The OAU was replaced by the African Union, which was launched in
questions.explanation: The AU was launched in Durban, South Africa, in July 2002.

questions.stem: The New Partnership for Africa's Development (NEPAD) was adopted mainly to
options: promote sustainable development and good governance in Africa
replace the United Nations in Africa
questions.explanation: NEPAD (2001) is an AU programme for development, with the African Peer Review Mechanism to promote good governance.

questions.stem: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was established in 1975 by the Treaty of
questions.explanation: The ECOWAS Treaty was signed in Lagos on 28 May 1975.

questions.stem: The headquarters of the ECOWAS Commission is in
questions.explanation: The ECOWAS Commission is based in Abuja, Nigeria.

questions.stem: In January 2025, the withdrawal of three Sahelian states from ECOWAS took effect. These states were
questions.explanation: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left ECOWAS and formed the Alliance of Sahel States, reducing ECOWAS to twelve members.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between power and authority. [4 marks]
(b) Explain five factors that can give a government legitimacy. [10 marks]
(c) State one way in which a government may lose legitimacy. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Power: the ability to make others act as one wishes, by force if necessary
2 marks: Authority: the recognised or lawful right to exercise power, accepted by the governed
2 marks: Free, fair and periodic elections
2 marks: Adherence to the constitution and the rule of law
2 marks: Performance: provision of security, welfare and services
2 marks: Respect for fundamental human rights
2 marks: Tradition/charisma, or recognition by other states and international bodies (any valid fifth factor)
1 mark: Any one: rigged elections, corruption, gross abuse of rights, failure to deliver services, unconstitutional seizure of power
questions.explanation: Power is the capacity to compel; authority is power accepted as rightful. Legitimacy flows from credible elections, constitutionalism, performance, respect for rights, tradition or charisma and external recognition. It is lost through rigging, corruption, repression or coups.

questions.stem:
(a) What is meant by the rule of law? [3 marks]
(b) Explain three principles of the rule of law as stated by A. V. Dicey. [6 marks]
(c) Highlight three limitations to the application of the rule of law in Nigeria. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Rule of law: supremacy of the law, under which all persons and authorities are subject to the law and government acts according to law
2 marks: Supremacy of the law: no one may be punished except for a breach of law established in the ordinary courts
2 marks: Equality before the law: all persons, whatever their status, are subject to the same law and courts
2 marks: Rights of the individual are secured by the ordinary law and decisions of the courts
2 marks: Immunity clause (section 308) for the President, Vice-President, Governors and Deputies
2 marks: Declaration of a state of emergency, which permits restriction of certain rights
2 marks: Diplomatic immunity, delegated legislation, illiteracy/poverty limiting access to courts, or executive lawlessness (any one valid)
questions.explanation: The rule of law means law is supreme and all are equal before it. Dicey's three pillars are supremacy of law, equality before the law and judicially protected rights. In Nigeria it is limited by immunity, emergency powers, diplomatic immunity, delegated legislation and poor access to justice.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the concept of separation of powers. [3 marks]
(b) With examples from the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, explain four ways in which checks and balances operate among the organs of government. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Separation of powers: the functions of government are divided among the legislature, executive and judiciary, each with separate personnel, to prevent tyranny (Montesquieu)
3 marks: The President can veto bills, but the National Assembly can override by a two-thirds majority
3 marks: The Senate confirms presidential nominees such as ministers, ambassadors and the Chief Justice
3 marks: The National Assembly approves the budget and can impeach the President for gross misconduct
3 marks: The courts can declare laws or executive actions unconstitutional through judicial review
questions.explanation: Separation of powers assigns law-making, execution and adjudication to different organs. Checks and balances let each restrain the others: veto and override, Senate confirmation, budget and impeachment powers, and judicial review.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a rigid and a flexible constitution. [4 marks]
(b) Give three advantages and two disadvantages of a rigid constitution. [10 marks]
(c) Name one country with a flexible constitution. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Rigid: can be amended only through a special and difficult procedure different from ordinary law-making
2 marks: Flexible: can be amended through the ordinary law-making process
2 marks: Advantage: provides stability and continuity
2 marks: Advantage: protects fundamental rights and minorities from hasty change
2 marks: Advantage: prevents manipulation by the ruling party
2 marks: Disadvantage: difficult to adapt to changing circumstances
2 marks: Disadvantage: delays needed reforms and may encourage unconstitutional change
1 mark: United Kingdom (or New Zealand)
questions.explanation: A rigid constitution, like Nigeria's, needs special majorities to amend; a flexible one, like Britain's, is amended like ordinary law. Rigidity brings stability and protects rights but slows adaptation.

questions.stem:
(a) Mention five functions of the legislature. [10 marks]
(b) Explain how the legislature in Nigeria controls public finance. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Making laws
2 marks: Approving the budget and appropriating funds
2 marks: Oversight of the executive through committees and investigations
2 marks: Confirming appointments made by the executive
2 marks: Impeachment of the chief executive, or amending the constitution, or representing constituents (any one)
2 marks: No money may be withdrawn from the Consolidated Revenue Fund except as authorised by an appropriation act passed by the legislature
2 marks: Public Accounts Committees examine the Auditor-General's reports on government spending
1 mark: The legislature approves supplementary budgets, loans and taxes
questions.explanation: The legislature makes laws, passes the budget, oversees and checks the executive, confirms appointments and may impeach. It controls finance through the appropriation process, public accounts committees and approval of taxes, loans and supplementary budgets.

questions.stem:
(a) What is meant by the independence of the judiciary? [3 marks]
(b) Explain four ways by which the independence of the judiciary is ensured in Nigeria. [8 marks]
(c) State two factors that may undermine judicial independence. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Judges are free to decide cases impartially according to law, without interference from the executive, legislature or any other person
2 marks: Appointment of judges on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council / Judicial Service Commissions
2 marks: Security of tenure: judges can be removed only by prescribed procedure for misconduct or inability
2 marks: Salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Revenue Fund
2 marks: Immunity of judges from legal action for acts done in their judicial capacity, or the requirement of legal qualifications and experience
2 marks: Executive interference in appointments or funding
2 marks: Corruption, or poor conditions of service, or disobedience of court orders by government
questions.explanation: Judicial independence means judges decide cases without pressure. It is protected by appointment through judicial councils, security of tenure, salaries charged on the Consolidated Revenue Fund and judicial immunity, but undermined by executive interference, corruption and disregard of court orders.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem:
(a) Define a federal system of government. [3 marks]
(b) Explain four features of a federal system. [8 marks]
(c) State two demerits of federalism. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: A system in which powers are constitutionally divided between a central government and component units, each independent in its own sphere
2 marks: A written and usually rigid constitution
2 marks: Division of powers (e.g. exclusive, concurrent and residual lists)
2 marks: Supremacy of the constitution with a court to settle disputes between levels
2 marks: Bicameral legislature or two/three levels of government
2 marks: It is expensive to operate because of duplication of institutions
2 marks: It may encourage conflicts over revenue and secessionist tendencies
questions.explanation: Federalism divides power between the centre and units by a supreme written constitution, with courts as umpire. It is costly and prone to friction over revenue and autonomy.

questions.topic: State Structure and Characteristics of Government
questions.stem:
(a) Explain five differences between the presidential and parliamentary systems of government. [10 marks]
(b) Give two merits and one demerit of the parliamentary system. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Presidential: one person is head of state and government; parliamentary: the two offices are separate
2 marks: Presidential: separation of powers; parliamentary: fusion of executive and legislature
2 marks: Presidential: fixed tenure; parliamentary: government can be removed by a vote of no confidence
2 marks: Presidential: ministers need not be legislators; parliamentary: ministers are members of parliament
2 marks: Presidential: President cannot dissolve the legislature; parliamentary: parliament can be dissolved before its term
2 marks: Merit: quick passage of government policies because the executive controls the legislature
1 mark: Merit: government is directly accountable to parliament through question time
2 marks: Demerit: possible dictatorship of the cabinet, or instability under weak coalitions
questions.explanation: The presidential system combines headships, separates powers and has fixed terms; the parliamentary system separates headships, fuses executive and legislature and depends on parliament's confidence. Parliamentary government is efficient and accountable but risks cabinet dictatorship or instability.

questions.stem:
(a) Define a political party. [3 marks]
(b) Explain four functions of political parties in a democracy. [8 marks]
(c) Give two differences between a political party and a pressure group. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: An organised group of people with similar ideas who seek to win elections and control the government to implement their programmes
2 marks: Sponsoring candidates for elections
2 marks: Political education and mobilisation of citizens
2 marks: Interest aggregation: combining various demands into policy programmes
2 marks: Forming the government or providing opposition and criticism
2 marks: A party seeks to control government; a pressure group only seeks to influence it
2 marks: A party contests elections; a pressure group does not field candidates (or: party has broad programmes, pressure group narrow interests)
questions.explanation: A political party is an organised group seeking power through elections. It nominates candidates, educates voters, aggregates interests, forms government or opposition. Unlike a pressure group, it contests elections to control government.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a pressure group? [3 marks]
(b) Explain four methods used by pressure groups to achieve their aims. [8 marks]
(c) State two factors that determine the effectiveness of a pressure group. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: An organised group of people with common interests that seeks to influence government policy without seeking to control government
2 marks: Lobbying legislators and officials
2 marks: Strikes, boycotts and peaceful demonstrations
2 marks: Use of the mass media and propaganda
2 marks: Litigation in court, or petitions and sponsoring of candidates indirectly
2 marks: Size, unity and financial strength of the membership
2 marks: Quality of leadership or the strategic importance of the group's members to the economy
questions.explanation: Pressure groups seek influence, not power. They use lobbying, strikes, media campaigns, petitions and court action. Their success depends on size, cohesion, funds, leadership and economic importance.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the meaning of the simple majority (first-past-the-post) electoral system. [3 marks]
(b) Give two advantages and two disadvantages of this system. [8 marks]
(c) Explain two conditions necessary for free and fair elections. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: The candidate who scores the highest number of valid votes in a constituency wins, even without an absolute majority
2 marks: Advantage: simple to understand and operate
2 marks: Advantage: results are known quickly and tend to produce stable governments
2 marks: Disadvantage: a candidate may win with a minority of total votes
2 marks: Disadvantage: small parties are under-represented and many votes are wasted
2 marks: An independent and impartial electoral body
2 marks: Secret ballot, universal adult suffrage, or freedom from violence and intimidation
questions.explanation: Under first-past-the-post the highest vote-getter wins. It is simple and decisive but can produce minority winners and wasted votes. Free elections need an independent electoral body, secret ballot, adult suffrage and a peaceful environment.

questions.stem:
(a) Mention five functions of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). [10 marks]
(b) Explain five constraints faced by INEC in the conduct of elections. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Organising, undertaking and supervising elections into federal and state offices
2 marks: Registering political parties
2 marks: Registration of voters and maintenance of the voters' register
2 marks: Monitoring the organisation, operation and finances of political parties
2 marks: Delimitation of constituencies, or voter education, or arranging for annual examination of party accounts
1 mark: Insecurity and violence
1 mark: Inadequate or late release of funds
1 mark: Logistics problems such as poor roads and late arrival of materials
1 mark: Vote buying and attempts by politicians to manipulate the process
1 mark: Voter apathy, or litigation, or technical failures of equipment
questions.explanation: INEC conducts federal and state elections, registers parties and voters, monitors party finances and delimits constituencies. Its work is hampered by insecurity, funding, logistics, vote buying, apathy and technical problems.

questions.stem:
(a) Define local government. [3 marks]
(b) Explain four functions of local governments in Nigeria. [8 marks]
(c) State two problems facing local governments in Nigeria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Government at the grassroots level, created by law, with powers to administer a defined area and provide services to the people
2 marks: Registration of births, deaths and marriages
2 marks: Construction and maintenance of markets, motor parks, local roads and drains
2 marks: Collection of rates, radio and television licences, and other local revenue
2 marks: Provision of primary health care and participation in primary education, or naming of streets
2 marks: Undue interference by state governments
2 marks: Inadequate funds, corruption, or shortage of skilled staff
questions.explanation: Local government is the third tier closest to the people. It registers vital events, maintains markets and local roads, collects local revenue and supports primary health and education. Problems include state interference, poor funding, corruption and staff shortages.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a public corporation? [3 marks]
(b) Explain three ways by which public corporations are controlled. [6 marks]
(c) Give three reasons why governments privatize public corporations. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: A government-owned enterprise established by statute to provide goods or services, managed by a board
2 marks: Ministerial control: the supervising minister appoints board members and gives policy directives
2 marks: Legislative control: through the enabling law, budget approval and investigation by committees
2 marks: Judicial control: corporations can be sued and their actions reviewed in court; or audit/public opinion
2 marks: To improve efficiency and service delivery
2 marks: To reduce the financial burden of subsidies on government
2 marks: To attract private investment and technology, or reduce corruption and political interference
questions.explanation: A public corporation is a statutory, state-owned enterprise. Ministers, the legislature, courts, auditors and the public control it. Privatization aims at efficiency, lower subsidy burdens and private investment.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the political organisation of the pre-colonial Yoruba (Oyo) political system. [9 marks]
(b) Explain three ways by which the powers of the Alaafin were checked. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: The Alaafin was the head of the empire and was regarded as sacred
2 marks: The Oyomesi, a council of seven led by the Bashorun, advised the Alaafin and acted as kingmakers
2 marks: The Are-Ona-Kakanfo commanded the army; the Ilari served as messengers and tax collectors
2 marks: Provincial towns were ruled by Obas or Baales who paid tribute to the Alaafin
1 mark: The Ogboni society served as a link and judicial body between the Alaafin and the Oyomesi
2 marks: The Oyomesi could present an empty calabash or parrot's eggs, requiring an unpopular Alaafin to commit suicide
2 marks: The Ogboni society checked both the Alaafin and the Oyomesi
2 marks: Customs and taboos, and the Ifa oracle, limited the Alaafin's actions
questions.explanation: Oyo was a centralized monarchy under the sacred Alaafin, advised by the Oyomesi under the Bashorun, with the Are-Ona-Kakanfo as army chief, Ilari as officials and provincial rulers paying tribute. The Oyomesi's power of rejection, the Ogboni and religious sanctions checked the Alaafin.

questions.stem:
(a) What is indirect rule? [3 marks]
(b) Give four reasons why the British adopted indirect rule in Nigeria. [8 marks]
(c) Explain two reasons why indirect rule failed in Eastern Nigeria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: A system of colonial administration in which the British governed through traditional rulers and institutions under the supervision of British officials
2 marks: Shortage of British administrative personnel
2 marks: Lack of funds to run direct administration
2 marks: Existence of a well-organised emirate system with taxation and courts in the North
2 marks: Language barrier, or desire to minimise resistance by using rulers the people already obeyed
2 marks: Absence of centralized traditional rulers, so the British created unpopular warrant chiefs
2 marks: Resistance to direct taxation and abuses by warrant chiefs, leading to the Aba Women's Riot of 1929
questions.explanation: Indirect rule governed through traditional authorities. It was adopted because of few officials, limited money, the ready emirate system and to reduce resistance. It failed in the East because the Igbo lacked centralized rulers and warrant chiefs were resented.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the French colonial policy of assimilation. [4 marks]
(b) Give three reasons why the policy of assimilation was abandoned. [6 marks]
(c) State five differences between British and French colonial administration in West Africa. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Assimilation aimed to turn Africans into French citizens in culture, language, law and outlook, treating colonies as overseas parts of France (e.g. the Four Communes of Senegal)
2 marks: It was expensive to provide French-style education and institutions for all
2 marks: Strong resistance from Africans, especially Muslims, who wished to keep their culture
2 marks: French citizens feared being outnumbered by African citizens in French politics
1 mark: British used indirect rule; French used direct, centralized rule
1 mark: British chiefs had real powers; French chiefs were mere agents
1 mark: British did not seek to make Africans British; French sought assimilation
1 mark: French colonies elected deputies to the French parliament; British colonies had local legislative councils
1 mark: French used forced labour and the indigenat system more widely; or federations (AOF) vs separate colonies
questions.explanation: Assimilation sought to make Africans French. It was dropped for cost, African resistance and French fears of being swamped. British rule was indirect and decentralized; French rule was direct, centralized, assimilationist and represented in Paris.

questions.stem:
(a) State five features of the Lyttleton Constitution of 1954. [10 marks]
(b) Explain why the Lyttleton Constitution is regarded as Nigeria's first federal constitution. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Established a federation of three regions, the Southern Cameroons and the Federal Territory of Lagos
2 marks: Division of powers into exclusive, concurrent and residual lists
2 marks: Introduced the office of Premier in the regions
2 marks: Regionalised the public service and the judiciary
2 marks: Introduced a Speaker for the House of Representatives, or direct elections into the federal House
3 marks: It constitutionally shared powers between the central government and the regions, each autonomous in its own sphere
2 marks: It created separate regional institutions (premiers, civil services and judiciaries) alongside federal ones
questions.explanation: The 1954 Lyttleton Constitution set up a federation with Lagos as federal territory, divided powers into exclusive, concurrent and residual lists, created premierships and regionalised the civil service and judiciary, making it Nigeria's first truly federal constitution.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain five reasons for military intervention in Nigerian politics. [10 marks]
(b) State five features of military rule. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Corruption among politicians
2 marks: Electoral malpractices and violence
2 marks: Ethnic and regional rivalry
2 marks: Economic mismanagement and hardship
2 marks: Personal ambition of officers, or breakdown of law and order, or influence of coups elsewhere
1 mark: Suspension of the constitution
1 mark: Rule by decrees and edicts
1 mark: Ban on political parties and activities
1 mark: Fusion of legislative and executive powers in a ruling council
1 mark: Centralized hierarchical command, or restriction of fundamental rights
questions.explanation: Coups were justified by corruption, rigged elections, ethnic conflict, economic decline and insecurity, alongside officers' ambitions. Military regimes suspended constitutions, ruled by decree, banned parties, fused powers and restricted rights.

questions.stem:
(a) State five aims of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). [10 marks]
(b) Highlight five problems facing ECOWAS. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Promote economic integration and cooperation among member states
2 marks: Free movement of persons, goods and services
2 marks: Removal of customs duties and trade barriers among members
2 marks: Common external tariff and harmonised policies in agriculture, industry and transport
2 marks: Raise living standards and promote peace and stability in the sub-region
1 mark: Political instability and coups in member states
1 mark: Withdrawal of some member states
1 mark: Language and colonial differences (Anglophone, Francophone, Lusophone)
1 mark: Multiple currencies and inadequate funding
1 mark: Poor infrastructure, or border restrictions, or dependence on foreign powers
questions.explanation: ECOWAS seeks economic integration, free movement, trade liberalisation, harmonised policies and regional peace. It is hampered by coups and withdrawals, linguistic and currency divisions, poor funding and infrastructure.
